  "text": "In the spring she had the eleventh tread repaired.

The carpenter brought his tools on a Tuesday and worked until noon. He asked whether she wanted the others done while he was there. Maren said only the one. He left a pale rectangle in the stair and a little heap of shavings, which she swept into a sack.

That night her foot rose too high. Nothing happened. She went on up.

There were other things to mend. The harbour office needed a gutter. Her kitchen window had swollen in its frame. For years she had lifted the kettle sideways to avoid the drip from the cupboard, and one morning she put the kettle down and fetched a screwdriver.

Erris still asked the time, though not every evening. Sometimes she was with other children. Once she passed Maren without seeing her, running after a boy who had taken her scarf. Maren heard them laughing beyond the fish shed.

At the end of May she went to the grave with a brush and a jar of water. She cleaned the letters of her mother's name. There was grass where the earth had been bare.

She stayed until her knees were damp, then took the jar home.

That night, after the three turns, she opened the log. Beneath the hour and the state of the tide she wrote: Stair repaired.

She considered adding the date of the work. It was already several weeks ago. She left the line as it stood.

Going down, she put her weight on the new board. It held without a sound."

  "text": "By August the new tread had darkened beneath her feet. A little pale wood remained at either end, where nobody stepped.

Erris came to the harbour office one afternoon carrying a clock wrapped in her scarf. It had belonged to her grandfather. She set it on the desk and asked whether Maren could make it go.

Maren said she knew very little about clocks.

But you always know the time, Erris said.

They took off the back. Inside were two screws lying loose and a spring that looked wrong to both of them. Maren found a saucer for the screws. They sat a while in the light from the open door.

There is a man inland, she said at last. We could ask him.

The following Thursday she left the office key with the carpenter and took the morning bus. Erris held the clock on her knees. Beyond the harbour road the land rose, and the sea disappeared before Maren had thought to look back.

The repairer kept the clock. They had an hour before the return bus and bought bread and cheese, which they ate on a bench outside the closed library. Erris read aloud the notices in the window.

When they came home the tide was out. Someone had put a bucket beneath the office gutter, though there had been no rain.

Maren carried it inside.

That evening she entered the tide and the hour. Then she turned back a page to check something, leaving a crumb of bread in the fold."

  "text": "The clock came back in September, in a box that had once held pears. The repairer had included the broken spring in an envelope. Erris tipped it into her palm, then put it away again.

At home it sounded louder than she remembered. For three nights she stopped it before bed. On the fourth she left it running.

Maren heard this account while clearing the harbour office shelf. There were receipts to bundle, a cracked cup to discard, and a key nobody could identify. Erris tried the key in the lower drawer. It fitted, but the drawer was already unlocked.

Inside lay a ruler and a map of the harbour before the outer wall was built. They spread the map on the desk, weighting one corner with the cup.

Erris put her finger on a small square beside the old road.

Was that a house?

A shed, Maren said. Your grandfather kept his nets there.

Erris studied the square for a moment, then moved the cup so she could see the rest of the road.

Later they carried the papers outside to shake the dust from them. The carpenter passed with his bicycle and asked whether the gutter had leaked.

Not yet, Maren said.

It will, he told her, and went on towards the boats.

She left the bucket where she could reach it.

Before closing, she swept beneath the desk. Among the dust was a hardened crumb. She brushed it into her hand and scattered the sweepings beyond the step.

Erris was waiting at the corner. Maren locked the door and caught up with her."
